questions.solution:
For a $2 \times 2$ determinant, multiply the main diagonal and subtract the other diagonal:

$(2)(5) - (3)(4) = 10 - 12 = \mathbf{-2}$.

Down-right minus down-left — the same cross pattern every time.

questions.q: If $A$ is a square matrix of order $3$ and $|A| = 5$, then $|2A|$ is:
questions.solution:
Multiplying a matrix by $k$ multiplies **every row** by $k$, and each row pulls a factor out of the determinant.

For order $n$: $|kA| = k^{n}|A|$. Here $|2A| = 2^{3} \times 5 = \mathbf{40}$.

A determinant is a volume. Double all three edges of a box and the volume grows eightfold, not twofold.

questions.q: For a square matrix $A$ of order $n$, $A\,(\text{adj }A)$ equals:
questions.solution:
$A\,(\text{adj }A) = (\text{adj }A)\,A = |A|\,I$ — this is the identity the whole inverse formula rests on.

Divide both sides by $|A|$ (when it is non-zero) and you get $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\,\text{adj }A$.

The adjoint is the inverse before it has been scaled down to size.

questions.q: If $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix with $|A| = 4$, then $|\text{adj }A|$ is:
questions.solution:
For order $n$, $|\text{adj }A| = |A|^{\,n-1}$.

Here $n = 3$, so $|\text{adj }A| = 4^{2} = \mathbf{16}$.

Quick derivation: take determinants of $A\,(\text{adj }A) = |A|I$ to get $|A| \cdot |\text{adj }A| = |A|^{3}$.

questions.q: The matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 3 & k \end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse when $k$ equals:
questions.solution:
A matrix has no inverse exactly when its determinant is zero (it is then called **singular**).

$|A| = 2k - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow k = \mathbf{6}$.

At $k = 6$ the second row is $1.5$ times the first — the rows point the same way, the 'area' they span collapses to zero, and nothing can be undone.

questions.q: Find the value of $x$ if $\begin{vmatrix} x & 2 \\ 18 & x \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 18 & 6 \end{vmatrix}$ and $x > 0$.
questions.solution:
Left side: $x^{2} - 36$. Right side: $36 - 36 = 0$.

$x^{2} - 36 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm 6$, and the question asks for the positive value, so $x = \mathbf{6}$.

questions.q: If $A$ is a square matrix with $|A| = 8$, find the value of $\left|A^{-1}\right| \times 8$.
questions.solution:
$AA^{-1} = I$, so $|A| \cdot \left|A^{-1}\right| = |I| = 1$, giving $\left|A^{-1}\right| = \dfrac{1}{|A|} = \dfrac18$.

Therefore $\left|A^{-1}\right| \times 8 = \mathbf{1}$.

The inverse shrinks volume by exactly the factor the matrix stretched it by — that is what undoing means.

$A_{23}$ deletes row 2 and column 3, leaving $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 7 & 8 \end{vmatrix} = 8 - 14 = -6$.

The cofactor carries the sign $(-1)^{2+3} = -1$, so $A_{23} = -(-6) = \mathbf{6}$.

The signs alternate like a chessboard starting with $+$ in the top-left corner — the minor tells you the size, the chessboard tells you the sign.

questions.q: Find the area (in square units) of the triangle whose vertices are $(1, 0)$, $(6, 0)$ and $(4, 3)$.
questions.solution:
Area $= \tfrac12\left|\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 6 & 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\right|$.

Expanding along the second column (two zeros there make it easy): only the $3$ contributes, with sign $(-1)^{3+2} = -1$:

$-3\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 6 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = -3(1 - 6) = 15$.

Area $= \tfrac12 \times 15 = \mathbf{7.5}$ square units.

**Check:** the base on the $x$-axis is $5$ and the height is $3$, so $\tfrac12 \times 5 \times 3 = 7.5$. ✓

questions.q: Find the value of $k$ for which the points $(2, -3)$, $(k, 2)$ and $(0, 7)$ are collinear.
questions.solution:
Three points are collinear exactly when the triangle they make has zero area, so set the determinant to zero:

$\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 & 1 \\ k & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$.

Expand along the first row:

$2(2 - 7) + 3(k - 0) + 1(7k - 0) = -10 + 3k + 7k = 10k - 10$.

$10k - 10 = 0 \Rightarrow k = \mathbf{1}$.

**Check with slopes:** from $(2, -3)$ to $(0, 7)$ the slope is $\dfrac{7 + 3}{0 - 2} = -5$, so the line is $y = 7 - 5x$; at $x = 1$ it gives $y = 2$. ✓

questions.q: For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, find $\text{adj }A$ and hence $A^{-1}$, and verify that $A\,(\text{adj }A) = |A|\,I$.
questions.solution:
$|A| = (2)(4) - (3)(1) = 5 \ne 0$, so the inverse exists.

For a $2 \times 2$ matrix the adjoint is a two-step trick: **swap the diagonal, flip the sign of the other two**.

$\text{adj }A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

$A\,(\text{adj }A) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix} = 5I = |A|\,I$. ✓

$A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

questions.q: Solve by the matrix method: $2x + 3y = 11$ and $x + 4y = 13$.
questions.solution:
Write it as $AX = B$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, $X = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix} 11 \\ 13 \end{pmatrix}$.

$|A| = 8 - 3 = 5 \ne 0$, so $X = A^{-1}B$ and the system has exactly one solution.

$A^{-1} = \tfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

$X = \tfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 11 \\ 13 \end{pmatrix} = \tfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 44 - 39 \\ -11 + 26 \end{pmatrix} = \tfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 15 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

$\mathbf{x = 1,\; y = 3}$. **Check:** $2(1) + 3(3) = 11$ ✓ and $1 + 4(3) = 13$ ✓.

questions.q: Using matrices, solve: $x + y + z = 6$, $y + 3z = 11$, $x + z = 2y$ (rearranged: $x - 2y + z = 0$).
questions.solution:
$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 11 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$.

**Determinant.** $|A| = 1(1 + 6) - 1(0 - 3) + 1(0 - 1) = 7 + 3 - 1 = 9 \ne 0$, so a unique solution exists.

**Elimination is quickest from here.** From the first equation $x = 6 - y - z$. Put that into the third:

$(6 - y - z) - 2y + z = 0 \Rightarrow 6 - 3y = 0 \Rightarrow y = 2$.

Then the second equation gives $2 + 3z = 11 \Rightarrow z = 3$, and the first gives $x = 6 - 2 - 3 = 1$.

$\mathbf{x = 1,\; y = 2,\; z = 3}$.

**Check all three:** $1+2+3 = 6$ ✓, $2 + 9 = 11$ ✓, $1 + 3 = 4 = 2(2)$ ✓.

The determinant is what licenses the answer: non-zero means the three planes meet at exactly one point.

questions.q: Evaluate $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ a^{2} & b^{2} & c^{2} \end{vmatrix}$ and state what it factorises to.
questions.solution:
Subtract column 1 from columns 2 and 3 ($C_2 \to C_2 - C_1$, $C_3 \to C_3 - C_1$) — a column operation of this kind leaves the value unchanged:

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a & b - a & c - a \\ a^{2} & b^{2} - a^{2} & c^{2} - a^{2} \end{vmatrix}$.

Expanding along the first row leaves a $2 \times 2$:

$(b-a)(c^{2}-a^{2}) - (c-a)(b^{2}-a^{2}) = (b-a)(c-a)\left[(c+a) - (b+a)\right] = (b-a)(c-a)(c-b)$.

So the value is $\mathbf{(b-a)(c-a)(c-b)}$, which is the same product as the usual form $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$ — two of the three sign flips cancel. This is the **Vandermonde** determinant, and it is zero exactly when two of $a$, $b$, $c$ are equal — two identical columns can never span any volume.

questions.q: Without expanding, explain why $\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 & 8 \\ 6s & 9 & 12 \end{vmatrix}$ is zero when $s = 1$.
questions.solution:
Put $s = 1$: the third row becomes $(6, 9, 12)$, which is exactly $3 \times (2, 3, 4)$ — three times the first row.

A determinant with one row a multiple of another is **zero**: pull the $3$ out of the row and you are left with two identical rows, and a determinant with two identical rows is zero.

Geometrically the three rows are three edges of a box, and two of them lie along the same line — the box is flat, so its volume is $\mathbf{0}$.
